Its erection must be positioned at such an inclination that it responds to the description of a Pythagorean right-angled triangle <note>original: "pythagoricum trigonum orthogonium"</note>; that is, the length should be divided into five parts, and the head of the screw should be raised by three of these parts, so that the space from the perpendicular line to its lower openings measures four parts. The method of how this should be done is described in the drawing at the end of this book.

<margin>
a. The screw <term>coclea</term> <gloss>spiral device/screw</gloss> erected according to the ratio of a Pythagorean triangle.
b. The beam <term>tigna</term> <gloss>supporting timber</gloss> in which the screw rotates.
</margin>

<note>A woodcut illustration shows an Archimedean screw used for irrigation or drainage. The device consists of a wooden shaft with an internal spiral encased in a cylinder, tilted at an angle. The lower end is submerged in water, and the upper end is supported by a tall wooden pillar. A large treadwheel is attached to the center of the shaft, allowing humans to turn the device by treading on its rungs. Water is shown being lifted through the screw and discharging from the top into a wooden trough or basin.</note>
